# 4. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

This section provides a systematic overview of the dataset including missing values, variable types, descriptive statistics, and distributional properties.

Missing value report

```{r}
na_report <- data.frame(
  variable = names(df),
  na_count = sapply(df, function(x) sum(is.na(x))),
  na_ratio = sapply(df, function(x) mean(is.na(x)))
)


na_report %>% 
  filter(na_count > 0) %>% 
  arrange(desc(na_ratio))
```

```{r}
numeric_summary <- numeric_vars %>%
pivot_longer(cols = everything(),
```

Distribution of numeric variables

```{r}
# 4.2 Distribution of key numeric variables (target + main predictors)

key_vars <- c(
  "Edevlet_Net_Gelir",   # Target: e-Government net income
  "HF_CUSTOMER_AGE",     # Age
  "KKB_SCORE",           # Credit bureau score
  "KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO"    # Credit card utilization
)

df %>%
  # Make sure these variables are numeric (in case they were read as character)
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(
      .cols = all_of(key_vars),
      .fns  = ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.x))
    )
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(all_of(key_vars)) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols      = everything(),
    names_to  = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  tidyr::drop_na() %>%
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = value)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title    = "Distribution of Key Numeric Variables",
    subtitle = "Income, age and KKB-related variables show clear skewness and potential outliers.",
    x        = "Value",
    y        = "Count"
  )
```

```{r}
# --- STEP 1: Prepare the Data Object ---
# We create a clean dataframe named 'model_data' first.
# This fixes the "object not found" error by ensuring the object exists.

model_data <- df %>%
  dplyr::select(
    Edevlet_Net_Gelir,     # Target Variable
    HF_CUSTOMER_AGE,       # Age
    KKB_SCORE,             # Credit Score
    Model_Gelir,           # Modeled Income
    KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO      # Credit Card Ratio
  ) %>%
  # Convert all selected columns to numeric
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) %>%
  # Clean masked values (replace -999... and placeholder dates with NA)
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ ifelse(. < -900000 | . == 19000101, NA, .))) %>%
  # Remove empty rows
  na.omit()

# --- STEP 2: Create the Plots ---

# Method 1: Zoomed Histogram (Income < 200,000 TL)

model_data %>%
  filter(Edevlet_Net_Gelir < 230000) %>%  # Filter out extreme outliers for better visibility
  ggplot(aes(x = Edevlet_Net_Gelir)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Income Distribution (Zoomed: < 200k TL)",
       subtitle = "Excluding extreme outliers",
       x = "Income (TL)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

# Method 2: Logarithmic Scale (Scientific Method)
# This allows us to see the entire distribution including outliers
ggplot(model_data, aes(x = Edevlet_Net_Gelir)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "orange", color = "white") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) + # Log transformation for skewed data
  labs(title = "Income Distribution (Logarithmic Scale)",
       subtitle = "Corrects for right-skewness",
       x = "Income (Log Scale)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Applying a log-scale to the income variable reveals a highly right-skewed distribution, with the majority of applicants concentrated around moderate income levels and a long right tail representing high-income individuals. This transformation is crucial for improving interpretability and model stability.

Restricting the range to incomes below 200,000 TL exposes the underlying clustering behavior caused by salary brackets and reporting patterns. The distribution still displays a heavy right skew even after removing extreme outliers.

```{r}
# --- 5. Lorenz Curve of Income (Inequality Analysis) ---

# Load package (do NOT reinstall inside the document)
library(ineq)

# Extract clean income vector from raw data
income_vec <- df$Edevlet_Net_Gelir %>% 
  as.numeric()

# Keep only positive, valid incomes
income_vec <- income_vec[ income_vec > 0 & !is.na(income_vec) ]

# Compute Lorenz curve
lorenz_obj <- Lc(income_vec)

# Plot Lorenz curve
plot(
  lorenz_obj,
  main = "Lorenz Curve of Household Income",
  xlab = "Cumulative Share of Customers",
  ylab = "Cumulative Share of Income",
  lwd  = 2,
  col  = "darkblue"
)

# Add equality line
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "red")

# Gini coefficient
gini_val <- ineq(income_vec, type = "Gini")
cat("Gini Coefficient:", round(gini_val, 3), "\n")


```

## 5.1 Boxplots of the target variable

```{r}
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)

# 1) Ana veri seti
df <- read_excel("data/synthetic_customers.xlsx")

rent_raw <- read_excel(
  "data/il_ortalama_kira.xlsx",
  sheet = "kira_verileri_canli_kayit"
)

# 3) İl bazında ortalama kira
kira_il <- rent_raw %>%
  transmute(
    il_upper = str_to_upper(Column1, locale = "tr"),
    kira_il  = readr::parse_number(
      Column3,
      locale = locale(decimal_mark = ",", grouping_mark = ".")
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(il_upper) %>%
  summarise(
    kira_il_ortalama = mean(kira_il, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# 4) Kira bilgilerini df'ye merge et
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    Il_upper = str_to_upper(`İkamet İl`, locale = "tr")
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    kira_il,
    by = c("Il_upper" = "il_upper")
  )

# 5) Kontrol – artık df'de kira_il_ortalama var mı?
names(df)[grepl("kira", names(df))]

df %>%
  dplyr::select(`İkamet İl`, Il_upper, kira_il_ortalama) %>%
  head()


```

```{r}
# --- 1. MASTER DATA PREPARATION (WIDE, CLEAN DATASET) ---

model_data_new <- df %>%
  dplyr::select(
    # --- Target variable ---
    Edevlet_Net_Gelir,
    
    # --- Core demographic and score variables ---
    HF_CUSTOMER_AGE,
    KKB_SCORE,
    HF_EDUCATION,
    HF_APPLICANT_EMPLOYMENT_STATUS,
    
    # --- Financial status and assets ---
    KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO,
    KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT,
    HF_AVG_ASSET_CURR_ACC_L3M,
    HF_ASSET_PRTCPATION_ACC_L3M,
    KKB_CUST_TENURE,
    HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari,
    
    # --- Application & location related variables ---
    KKB_TOT_APP_CNT_L12M,
    `İkamet İl`,
    Tier,
    HF_APPLICANT_PROFESSION_CODE,
    
    # --- Detailed KKB variables used in ML models ---
    KKB_CC_OPEN_MAX_LIM_AMT,
    KKB_CL_TOT_RISK_AMT,
    KKB_MORTG_TOT_RISK_AMT,
    KKB_CC_TOT_MONTHLY_PAYM_AMT,
    KKB_NON_DELQ_ACCT_CNT,
    KKB_CC_OPEN_CNT,
    KKB_CC_ACCT_CNT,
    KKB_CURR_DELQ_DAY_CNT,
    KKB_CURR_TOT_FOLLOW_AMT,
    KKB_DELQ_ACCT_CNT,

    
    # --- New rent feature merged from external file ---
    kira_il_ortalama
  ) %>%
  
  # 1) Clean income: cast to numeric and remove clearly invalid or low values
  mutate(
    Edevlet_Net_Gelir = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(Edevlet_Net_Gelir))
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(Edevlet_Net_Gelir),
    Edevlet_Net_Gelir >= 23000      # exclude very low reported income
  ) %>%
  
  # 2) Convert numeric-like character columns to numeric
  mutate(across(
    c(
      HF_CUSTOMER_AGE,
      KKB_SCORE,
      KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO,
      KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT,
      HF_AVG_ASSET_CURR_ACC_L3M,
      KKB_CUST_TENURE,
      HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari,
      KKB_TOT_APP_CNT_L12M,
      KKB_CC_OPEN_MAX_LIM_AMT,
      KKB_CL_TOT_RISK_AMT,
      KKB_MORTG_TOT_RISK_AMT,
      KKB_CC_TOT_MONTHLY_PAYM_AMT,
      KKB_NON_DELQ_ACCT_CNT,
      KKB_CC_OPEN_CNT,
      KKB_CC_ACCT_CNT,
      KKB_CURR_DELQ_DAY_CNT,
      KKB_CURR_TOT_FOLLOW_AMT,
      KKB_DELQ_ACCT_CNT,
      kira_il_ortalama
    ),
    ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(.)))
  )) %>%
  
  # 3) Replace masked / sentinel values with NA
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.numeric),
      ~ ifelse(. < -900000 | . == 19000101, NA, .)
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # 4) Drop rows with missing values
  #    (required for standard linear regression)
  na.omit()


# --- 2. STANDARDIZATION, LOG-TRANSFORMS AND FEATURE ENGINEERING ---

model_data_scaled <- model_data_new %>%
  mutate(
    # 1) Ensure all continuous variables are numeric (defensive casting)
    Edevlet_Net_Gelir            = as.numeric(Edevlet_Net_Gelir),
    HF_CUSTOMER_AGE              = as.numeric(HF_CUSTOMER_AGE),
    KKB_SCORE                    = as.numeric(KKB_SCORE),
    KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO            = as.numeric(KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO),
    KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT      = as.numeric(KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT),
    HF_AVG_ASSET_CURR_ACC_L3M    = as.numeric(HF_AVG_ASSET_CURR_ACC_L3M),
    HF_ASSET_PRTCPATION_ACC_L3M  = as.numeric(HF_ASSET_PRTCPATION_ACC_L3M),
    KKB_CUST_TENURE              = as.numeric(KKB_CUST_TENURE),
    HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari = as.numeric(HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari),
    KKB_TOT_APP_CNT_L12M         = as.numeric(KKB_TOT_APP_CNT_L12M),
    KKB_CC_OPEN_MAX_LIM_AMT      = as.numeric(KKB_CC_OPEN_MAX_LIM_AMT),
    KKB_CL_TOT_RISK_AMT          = as.numeric(KKB_CL_TOT_RISK_AMT),
    KKB_MORTG_TOT_RISK_AMT       = as.numeric(KKB_MORTG_TOT_RISK_AMT),
    KKB_CC_TOT_MONTHLY_PAYM_AMT  = as.numeric(KKB_CC_TOT_MONTHLY_PAYM_AMT),
    KKB_NON_DELQ_ACCT_CNT        = as.numeric(KKB_NON_DELQ_ACCT_CNT),
    KKB_CC_OPEN_CNT              = as.numeric(KKB_CC_OPEN_CNT),
    KKB_CC_ACCT_CNT              = as.numeric(KKB_CC_ACCT_CNT),
    KKB_CURR_DELQ_DAY_CNT        = as.numeric(KKB_CURR_DELQ_DAY_CNT),
    KKB_CURR_TOT_FOLLOW_AMT      = as.numeric(KKB_CURR_TOT_FOLLOW_AMT),
    kira_il_ortalama             = as.numeric(kira_il_ortalama)
  ) %>%
  
  # 2) Keep only strictly positive income values for log-transform
  filter(
    !is.na(Edevlet_Net_Gelir),
    Edevlet_Net_Gelir > 0
  ) %>%
  
  mutate(
    # 3) Log-transformed target (used in linear regression models)
    log_income = log(Edevlet_Net_Gelir),
    
    # 4) Log-transformed rent feature (log(1 + x) to handle zeros)
    t_RentIl   = log1p(kira_il_ortalama),
    
    # 5) Z-score standardization of key continuous predictors
    z_HF_CUSTOMER_AGE              = as.numeric(scale(HF_CUSTOMER_AGE)),
    z_KKB_SCORE                    = as.numeric(scale(KKB_SCORE)),
    z_KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO            = as.numeric(scale(KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO)),
    z_KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT      = as.numeric(scale(KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT)),
    z_HF_AVG_ASSET_CURR_ACC_L3M    = as.numeric(scale(HF_AVG_ASSET_CURR_ACC_L3M)),
    z_HF_ASSET_PRTCPATION_ACC_L3M  = as.numeric(scale(HF_ASSET_PRTCPATION_ACC_L3M)),
    z_KKB_CUST_TENURE              = as.numeric(scale(KKB_CUST_TENURE)),
    z_HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari = as.numeric(scale(HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari)),
    z_KKB_TOT_APP_CNT_L12M         = as.numeric(scale(KKB_TOT_APP_CNT_L12M)),
    z_KKB_CC_OPEN_MAX_LIM_AMT      = as.numeric(scale(KKB_CC_OPEN_MAX_LIM_AMT)),
    z_KKB_CL_TOT_RISK_AMT          = as.numeric(scale(KKB_CL_TOT_RISK_AMT)),
    z_KKB_MORTG_TOT_RISK_AMT       = as.numeric(scale(KKB_MORTG_TOT_RISK_AMT)),
    z_KKB_CC_TOT_MONTHLY_PAYM_AMT  = as.numeric(scale(KKB_CC_TOT_MONTHLY_PAYM_AMT)),
    z_KKB_NON_DELQ_ACCT_CNT        = as.numeric(scale(KKB_NON_DELQ_ACCT_CNT)),
    z_KKB_CC_OPEN_CNT              = as.numeric(scale(KKB_CC_OPEN_CNT)),
    z_KKB_CC_ACCT_CNT              = as.numeric(scale(KKB_CC_ACCT_CNT)),
    z_KKB_CURR_DELQ_DAY_CNT        = as.numeric(scale(KKB_CURR_DELQ_DAY_CNT)),
    z_KKB_CURR_TOT_FOLLOW_AMT      = as.numeric(scale(KKB_CURR_TOT_FOLLOW_AMT)),
    
    # 6) Short aliases (for more readable model formulas)
    z_Age    = z_HF_CUSTOMER_AGE,
    z_Score  = z_KKB_SCORE,
    z_Util   = z_KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO,
    z_Limit  = z_KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT,
    z_Asset  = z_HF_AVG_ASSET_CURR_ACC_L3M,
    z_Tenure = z_KKB_CUST_TENURE,
    
    # 7) Additional engineered numeric features
    t_PaymentCap = log(HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari + 1),
    z_AppCount   = as.numeric(scale(KKB_TOT_APP_CNT_L12M)),
    t_MaxLimit   = log1p(KKB_CC_OPEN_MAX_LIM_AMT),
    t_FollowAmt  = log1p(KKB_CURR_TOT_FOLLOW_AMT),
    t_RiskAmt    = log1p(KKB_CL_TOT_RISK_AMT),
    
    # 8) City grouping: İstanbul, Ankara, İzmir vs Other
    f_City = factor(
      ifelse(`İkamet İl` %in% c("İSTANBUL", "ANKARA", "İZMİR"),
             `İkamet İl`, "Other")
    ),
    
    # 9) Categorical encodings (factors for regression / ML)
    f_Education  = as.factor(HF_EDUCATION),
    f_EmpStatus  = as.factor(HF_APPLICANT_EMPLOYMENT_STATUS),
    f_Tier       = as.factor(Tier)
  ) %>%
  
  # 10) Final NA removal for modeling
  na.omit()


```

The boxplot summarizes the central tendency and extreme values of income using a log-scaled axis to correct for right-skewness. While the box occupies the middle range of the distribution, numerous outliers appear on both ends due to the highly discrete and heavy-tailed structure of the income variable. The unusual appearance is expected: income is not continuous and is frequently reported in fixed brackets, causing many identical values to fall outside the whiskers. Despite this, the boxplot effectively highlights the skewness and presence of extreme values in the dataset.

The violin plot visualizes the full density of the income distribution on a logarithmic scale. Because income values in this dataset fall into discrete salary tiers rather than forming a smooth continuous distribution, the violin plot captures these clusters more accurately than a boxplot. The plot clearly displays a concentrated mass of mid-income applicants and a long right tail representing higher-income individuals. The multiple “bulges’’ along the violin reflect the banded, discretized nature of reported income.

```{r}
model_data %>%
  filter(edevlet_net_gelir > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = edevlet_net_gelir)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Income Distribution – Violin Plot (Log Scale)",
    subtitle = "Violin plots handle discrete income levels much better",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Income (log scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

## 5.2 Bivariate relationships with income

The scatterplots and LOESS curves indicate clear non-linear patterns between income and predictors such as age, credit card utilization and KKB score. Therefore, relying on a simple linear fit is inadequate. Based on these patterns, transformations such as Age², log-limit, log-utilization, and √score were deemed necessary to linearize relationships before model estimation.

# **6.0 Full Multiple Regression Model (ALL Predictors NEW)**

In this section, we fit a multiple linear regression model using **all available predictors** in the dataset.\
The goal is to:

1.  Use the full feature set (after cleaning and preprocessing),

2.  Quantify the overall explanatory power of all predictors together,

3.  Diagnose multicollinearity and model assumptions,

4.  Justify the need for later feature reduction and model refinement.

```{r}

# 5.0 – Clean master dataset 

df_master <- df %>%

  mutate(Edevlet_Net_Gelir = as.numeric(Edevlet_Net_Gelir)) %>%

  filter(!is.na(Edevlet_Net_Gelir),
         Edevlet_Net_Gelir >= 23000) %>%

  mutate(across(
    c(
      HF_CUSTOMER_AGE,
      KKB_SCORE,
      KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO,
      KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT,
      HF_AVG_ASSET_CURR_ACC_L3M,
      HF_ASSET_PRTCPATION_ACC_L3M,
      KKB_CUST_TENURE,
      HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari,
      KKB_TOT_APP_CNT_L12M,
      KKB_CC_OPEN_MAX_LIM_AMT,
      KKB_CL_TOT_RISK_AMT,
      KKB_MORTG_TOT_RISK_AMT,
      KKB_CC_TOT_MONTHLY_PAYM_AMT,
      KKB_NON_DELQ_ACCT_CNT,
      KKB_CC_OPEN_CNT,
      KKB_CC_ACCT_CNT,
      KKB_CURR_DELQ_DAY_CNT,
      KKB_CURR_TOT_FOLLOW_AMT
    ),
    ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.))
  )) %>%
  # Masked değerleri temizle
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric),
                ~ ifelse(. < -900000 | . == 19000101, NA, .))) %>%
  # E-devlet değişkenlerinden sadece target'ı bırak
  {
    ede_cols  <- grep("^Edevlet_", names(.), value = TRUE)
    ede_drop  <- setdiff(ede_cols, "Edevlet_Net_Gelir")
    dplyr::select(., -all_of(ede_drop))
  } %>%
  # Leakage / teknik kolonları at
  dplyr::select(
    -starts_with("Model_"),
    -starts_with("Beyan_"),
    -starts_with("Final"),
    -matches("(?i)karar"),
    -matches("(?i)hash"),
    -matches("(?i)ref")
  ) %>%
  # Target'ı başa al
  dplyr::select(Edevlet_Net_Gelir, dplyr::everything()) %>%
  # Tamamen NA'lı satırları at
  na.omit()

df_master <- df_master %>%
  left_join(
    kira_il,
    by = c("İkamet İl" = "il_upper")
  ) %>%
  filter(Edevlet_Net_Gelir > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    log_income = log(Edevlet_Net_Gelir)
  )

df_master %>%
  distinct(`İkamet İl`) %>%
  anti_join(kira_il, by = c("İkamet İl" = "il_upper"))



df_master <- df_master %>%
  filter(Edevlet_Net_Gelir > 0) %>%             # güvenlik amaçlı
  mutate(
    log_income = log(Edevlet_Net_Gelir)
  )




```

```{r}


df_full <- df_master   

full_rec <- recipe(Edevlet_Net_Gelir ~ ., data = df_master) %>%
  step_log(all_outcomes()) %>%
  step_rm(Edevlet_Net_Gelir) %>%                     
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%   
  step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors(), new_level = "missing") %>% 
  step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), threshold = 0.02) %>% 
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>% 
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>% 
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

full_prep <- prep(full_rec)
full_data <- juice(full_prep)

print(dim(full_data))

if (nrow(full_data) > ncol(full_data)) {
  full_lm_all <- lm(log_income ~ ., data = full_data)
  summary(full_lm_all)
} else {
  message("Full OLS is saturated (p >> n); used only as diagnostic. 
Proceed to LASSO in Section 6.2 for variable selection.")
}


```

The full OLS model becomes saturated after dummy encoding, resulting in more predictors than observations.\
This leads to zero residual degrees of freedom and undefined coefficient statistics (NaN standard errors and t-values).\
Such behavior is expected in high-dimensional datasets and highlights severe multicollinearity and overparameterization.\
Therefore, the full model is useful only as a diagnostic starting point and strongly motivates variable reduction techniques such as stepwise AIC, regularization (LASSO), and tree-based ML models.

## 6.0.1 Diagnostics for the Full Model

```{r}
# Optional: basic dimension diagnostics
n_obs    <- nrow(full_data)
n_params <- length(coef(full_lm_all))
model_rank <- full_lm_all$rank

cat("Number of observations: ", n_obs, "\n")
cat("Number of parameters (incl. intercept): ", n_params, "\n")
cat("Model rank: ", model_rank, "\n")


```

Three predictors were aliased (perfectly collinear with other regressors) and were removed before computing VIF values. VIF diagnostics indicate substantial multicollinearity among several credit and income variables, which is expected given the highly engineered banking dataset.

```{r}
# --- 6.1.1 Multicollinearity Diagnostics (Aliasing + VIF) ---

library(car)

# 1. Find aliased (perfectly collinear) terms
aliased_terms <- names(coef(full_lm_all))[is.na(coef(full_lm_all))]
aliased_terms

# 2. Refit model without aliased predictors
full_lm_noalias <- update(
  full_lm_all,
  as.formula(
    paste("log_income ~ . -", paste(aliased_terms, collapse = " - "))
  )
)

# 3. VIFs on de-aliased model
vif_full <- vif(full_lm_noalias)

summary(vif_full)
sort(vif_full, decreasing = TRUE)[1:20]


```

Instead of manually dropping high-VIF predictors, we relied on LASSO as a data-driven screening tool.\
LASSO was first applied on the full dummy-encoded design matrix, and we retained only predictors with non-zero coefficients.\
This two-step procedure preserves interpretability (standard errors, t-statistics, F-tests) while controlling multicollinearity in a principled way.

```{r}
# 1) Select numeric columns
df_num <- df_master %>%
  mutate(Edevlet_Net_Gelir = as.numeric(Edevlet_Net_Gelir))

df_num <- df_num[, sapply(df_num, is.numeric)]

# 2) Define Target
y_income <- df_num$Edevlet_Net_Gelir

# 3) Define Leakage Patterns
# We exclude columns that imply the target or post-decision outcomes.
remove_patterns <- c(
  "log_income",
  "^Final",
  "^Model",
  "^Beyan",
  "^Edevlet_", # Exclude other E-devlet fields
  "^Ihtiyac",
  "Gelir"      # Exclude other income fields
)

# 4) Safely remove target and leakage columns
cols_to_remove <- c("Edevlet_Net_Gelir", "ID")
cols_to_remove <- intersect(cols_to_remove, names(df_num))

predictor_df <- df_num %>%
  dplyr::select(
    -all_of(cols_to_remove),
    -dplyr::matches(paste(remove_patterns, collapse = "|"))
  )

# 5) Calculate Correlations
corr_df <- predictor_df %>%
  summarise(across(everything(),
                   ~ cor(.x, y_income, use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "correlation"
  ) %>%
  mutate(abs_corr = abs(correlation)) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs_corr)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 30)

# 6) List Top 30 Variables
print(corr_df$variable)

# 7) Visualize with Heatmap
ggplot(corr_df,
       aes(x = "Edevlet_Net_Gelir",
           y = reorder(variable, correlation),
           fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "darkred",
    mid = "white",
    high = "darkblue",
    midpoint = 0
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 30 Correlations with Actual Income",
    subtitle = "Variables ranked by absolute correlation (Leakage variables removed)",
    x = "",
    y = "Predictor",
    fill = "Corr"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

## 6.0.2 LASSO Regression with Feature Selection (UPDATED)

**t_PaymentCap** represents the log-transformed monthly installment capacity. Tree-based models identified payment capacity as the dominant predictive signal,so we engineered a smooth transformation that LASSO could capture.This explains why t_PaymentCap emerges as the strongest predictor in the linear model.

```{r}


lasso_rec <- recipe(log_income ~ ., data = model_data_scaled) %>%
  
  # 1) Remove target + leakage variables
  step_rm(
    Edevlet_Net_Gelir, 
    starts_with("Edevlet_"),
    starts_with("Model_"),
    starts_with("Beyan_"),
    matches("(?i)final"),
    matches("(?i)karar")
  ) %>%
  
  # 2) Simplify high-cardinality categoricals
  step_other(f_Education, threshold = 0.03) %>%
  step_other(f_EmpStatus, threshold = 0.03) %>%
  step_other(f_City,      threshold = 0.03) %>%
  step_other(f_Tier,      threshold = 0.03) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  
  # 3) Hand-crafted non-linear & interaction features
  step_mutate(
    # A) Ratio-based credit capacity features
    avg_limit_per_card = KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT / pmax(KKB_CC_OPEN_CNT, 1),
    limit_ratio        = KKB_CC_OPEN_MAX_LIM_AMT / pmax(KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT, 1),
    taksit_yuk_oran    = HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari / pmax(KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT, 1),

    # B) Limit-based segmentation thresholds (numeric flags)
    t_lim_mid  = if_else(KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT >  50000, 1, 0),
    t_lim_high = if_else(KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT > 100000, 1, 0),
    t_lim_vip  = if_else(KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT > 200000, 1, 0),

    # C) Non-linear transforms the trees hinted at
    age2          = z_Age^2,
    log_limit_raw = log(KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT + 1),
    log_util_raw  = log(KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO + 0.001),
    sqrt_score    = sqrt(KKB_SCORE),

    # D) Interaction between payment capacity and normalized limit
    paycap_x_limit = t_PaymentCap * z_Limit
  ) %>%
  
  # 4) Drop zero-variance predictors
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  
  # 5) Standardize all numeric predictors (required for LASSO)
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())


# LASSO specification (fixed penalty here; can also be tuned via grid)
lasso_spec <- linear_reg(
  penalty = 0.01,
  mixture = 1          # mixture = 1 → pure LASSO (L1 penalty)
) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

lasso_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(lasso_rec) %>%
  add_model(lasso_spec)

# Fit LASSO on the prepared data
lasso_fit <- fit(lasso_wf, data = model_data_scaled)

# Extract non-zero coefficients selected by LASSO
lasso_fit_parsnip <- extract_fit_parsnip(lasso_fit)

lasso_results <- tidy(lasso_fit_parsnip) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)", estimate != 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(estimate)))

cat("\n--- Selected Predictors by LASSO (λ = 0.01) ---\n")
print(lasso_results)

# Plot the top 20 selected predictors by absolute coefficient size
lasso_results %>%
  slice_head(n = 20) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(term, estimate), y = estimate, fill = estimate > 0)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title    = "LASSO Regression: Top 20 Predictors",
    subtitle = "E-government income variables excluded; selection is based on KKB & HF features only",
    x        = "Variable",
    y        = "Coefficient Estimate",
    fill     = "Positive Effect"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation of LASSO Results**

The LASSO model, estimated after excluding all e-Government variables and potential leakage features, produced a compact set of predictors driven entirely by KKB and HF operational data. The strongest positive contributors to predicted income were *HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari*, *Basvuru_Skoru*, and several credit-behavior indicators such as *KKB_Risk_L12M* and *KKB_NON_DELQ_ACCT_CNT*. These variables capture repayment capacity, borrowing discipline, and overall creditworthiness—attributes typically associated with higher-income applicants. In contrast, negative coefficients emerged for features reflecting existing financial burden or elevated risk levels, including *HF_APP_INST_AMT*, KKB delinquency metrics, lower-tier customer segments (e.g., Tier T5/T6), and asset-related volatility measures. Overall, the LASSO framework effectively removed multicollinearity and retained only the most informative, stable predictors. The resulting feature set indicates that income variation in the absence of e-Government data is primarily explained by repayment ability, historical credit performance, and customer risk tier, making these variables strong candidates for downstream modeling and business decision-making.

## 6.0.3 LASSO-Screened Reduced OLS Model

To translate the LASSO screening into a more interpretable and regulation-friendly specification, we re-estimated a standard OLS model using only the predictors selected by LASSO. Concretely, we first applied the LASSO recipe (with dummy encoding and standardization) to obtain a reduced design matrix and then retained only variables with non-zero LASSO coefficients. Starting from this compact set, we iteratively removed aliased predictors and dropped the worst high-VIF terms until all remaining regressors satisfied a conservative multicollinearity threshold (VIF ≤ 10).

```{r}
# --- LASSO → Reduced OLS Helper Function (Clean & Working Version) ---

build_reduced_ols <- function(lasso_rec, lasso_results, vif_threshold = 10) {
  
  library(dplyr)
  library(broom)
  library(car)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(recipes)
  
  cat("\n[1] Preparing design matrix from LASSO recipe...\n")
  lasso_prep  <- prep(lasso_rec, training = model_data_scaled)
  design_data <- juice(lasso_prep)
  
  if (!"log_income" %in% names(design_data)) {
    stop("`log_income` must be present in the design matrix as the outcome.")
  }
  
  # --- 2. Extract non-zero LASSO coefficients ---
  cat("\n[2] Extracting non-zero LASSO coefficients...\n")
  selected_terms <- lasso_results %>%
    filter(term != "(Intercept)", estimate != 0) %>%
    pull(term) %>%
    unique()
  
  keep_terms <- intersect(selected_terms, colnames(design_data))
  cat("   → LASSO selected", length(selected_terms), "vars. Found", 
      length(keep_terms), "in design matrix.\n")
  
  df_reduced <- design_data %>%
    dplyr::select(log_income, all_of(keep_terms))
  
  # --- 3. Fit initial OLS ---
  cat("\n[3] Fitting initial Reduced OLS model...\n")
  ols_fit <- lm(log_income ~ ., data = df_reduced)
  
  # --- 4. Remove aliased terms ---
  aliased_terms <- names(coef(ols_fit))[is.na(coef(ols_fit))]
  if (length(aliased_terms) > 0) {
    cat("   → Removing aliased terms:\n")
    print(aliased_terms)
    ols_fit <- update(ols_fit, as.formula(
      paste("log_income ~ . -", paste(aliased_terms, collapse = " - "))
    ))
  }
  
  # --- 5. Iterative VIF reduction ---
  cat("\n[4] Iterative VIF reduction (threshold =", vif_threshold, ")...\n")
  repeat {
    vifs <- tryCatch(car::vif(ols_fit), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(vifs)) break
    
    high_vifs <- names(vifs)[vifs > vif_threshold]
    if (length(high_vifs) == 0) {
      cat("   → All predictors below VIF threshold.\n")
      break
    }
    
    var_to_drop <- high_vifs[which.max(vifs[high_vifs])]
    cat("   → Dropping", var_to_drop, "with VIF =", round(vifs[var_to_drop], 2), "\n")
    ols_fit <- update(ols_fit, as.formula(paste("log_income ~ . -", var_to_drop)))
  }
  
  # --- 6. Final model summary ---
  cat("\n[5] Final Reduced OLS model summary:\n")
  print(summary(ols_fit))
  
  # --- 7. Coefficient Plot ---
  ols_tidy <- broom::tidy(ols_fit) %>% arrange(p.value)
  
  coef_plot <- ols_tidy %>%
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
    slice_head(n = 20) %>%
    mutate(signif = p.value < 0.05, 
           term = reorder(term, estimate)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = term, y = estimate, fill = signif)) +
    geom_col() +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(title = "Final OLS Coefficients (LASSO → VIF Cleaned)",
         x = "Predictor", y = "Coefficient", fill = "Significant?") +
    theme_minimal()
  
  print(coef_plot)
  
  # --- Return outputs ---
  return(invisible(list(
    model = ols_fit,
    data  = df_reduced,
    tidy  = ols_tidy
  )))
}



# Build Reduced OLS model based on LASSO-selected predictors
reduced_ols_result <- build_reduced_ols(
  lasso_rec     = lasso_rec,

  lasso_results = lasso_results,
  vif_threshold = 10
)

# Extract and inspect final OLS model
reduced_ols_model <- reduced_ols_result$model
summary(reduced_ols_model)

```

The reduced OLS model, constructed by screening variables through LASSO and then eliminating multicollinearity via iterative VIF reduction, highlights a concise set of predictors that explain variation in log-income without relying on any e-Government fields or post-decision information.

The strongest positive contributors are **HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari**, **Başvuru_Skoru**, **Talep_Limit**, and recent credit-risk measures such as **KKB_Risk_L12M** and **KKB_NON_DELQ_ACCT_CNT**. These variables collectively capture repayment capacity, the applicant’s internal creditworthiness assessment, and consistent repayment behavior—factors typically associated with higher reported income.

Negative coefficients are dominated by delinquency-related and burden-related indicators, including **KKB_ALL_CC_DELQ_CNT_L12M**, **KKB_CURR_CC_DELQ_AMT**, and **HF_APP_INST_AMT**, as well as higher-risk customer tiers (**Tier_T5**, **Tier_T6**). These features reflect financial stress, accumulated obligations, and subsegment risk classifications, which are logically associated with lower income profiles.

## 6.1 Base modelling dataset

## 

We exclude all observations with income below 23,000 TL, since these values are implausible in practice and most likely correspond to under-reported or erroneous entries. Including them would distort the income distribution and harm model performance.

### 6.1 Base model (no interactions yet)

```{r}
# 6.1 – Updated Full Multiple Regression Model

full_model <- lm(
  log_income ~ 
    
    # --- Core life-cycle effects ---
    z_Age + I(z_Age^2) +
    
    # --- Core creditworthiness predictors ---
    z_Score +
    z_Util +
    z_Limit +
    z_Asset +
    z_Tenure +
    
    # --- Engineered numeric predictors ---

    z_AppCount +           # Application intensity
    t_MaxLimit +           # Max CC limit (log)
    t_FollowAmt +          # Follow-up balance (log)
    t_RiskAmt +            # Consumer-loan risk (log)
    
    # --- Additional standardized behavioural variables ---
    z_KKB_CC_OPEN_MAX_LIM_AMT +
    z_KKB_CC_OPEN_CNT +
    z_KKB_CC_ACCT_CNT +
    z_KKB_CURR_DELQ_DAY_CNT +
    z_KKB_NON_DELQ_ACCT_CNT +

    z_KKB_MORTG_TOT_RISK_AMT +
    z_KKB_CL_TOT_RISK_AMT +
    
    # --- Categorical predictors ---
    f_Education +
    f_EmpStatus +
    f_City +
    f_Tier +

    
    
    # --- Interaction: education modifies age slope ---
    f_Education * z_Age,
  
  data = model_data_scaled
)

summary(full_model)


```

The base model uses log-transformed income as the dependent variable and combines standardized numeric predictors (age, age squared, KKB score, credit card utilization and customer tenure) with key categorical descriptors (education, employment status and job title). **Age enters the model both linearly and quadratically** to allow for a non-linear income profile over the life cycle.

Coefficients for the main numeric predictors are generally statistically significant and have the expected signs: higher KKB score and longer customer tenure are associated with higher reported income, whereas extreme credit card utilization may be linked to specific risk segments. The categorical effects capture structural differences across education and occupation groups that are not explained by pure credit history. Overall, the base model explains a non-trivial share of the variation in log-income while remaining interpretable and aligned with business intuition.

#### 6.2.1 Overall Model Utility Test

```{r}


#The goal of this test is to examine whether the predictors jointly contribute to explaining variation in log-income. We test:

#- **H₀:** All slope coefficients are equal to zero  
#- **H₁:** At least one slope coefficient is nonzero  

#Below we compute the F-statistic, degrees of freedom, and p-value.

# --- Overall Model Utility Test ---

lm_sum <- summary(lm_fit)

# Extract F-stat components
f_stat  <- lm_sum$fstatistic[1]
df1     <- lm_sum$fstatistic[2]
df2     <- lm_sum$fstatistic[3]

# Compute p-value
p_value <- pf(f_stat, df1, df2, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Print clean output
cat("\n--- Overall Model Utility Test ---\n")
cat("F(", df1, ", ", df2, ") = ", round(f_stat, 2),
    ", p-value = ", signif(p_value, 4), "\n", sep = "")


```

The overall model utility test evaluates whether all slope coefficients are simultaneously equal to zero, implying that none of the predictors improve the explanation of log-income beyond the intercept-only baseline. The estimated statistic, F(17,820)=2.99F(17, 820) = 2.99F(17,820)=2.99, yields a p-value of 4.47×10−54.47\times10\^{-5}4.47×10−5, which is well below the 0.05 significance threshold.The overall F-test strongly rejects the null hypothesis that all slope coefficients are jointly equal to zero (p \< 0.001). This confirms that the set of predictors provides statistically significant explanatory power for log-income relative to an intercept-only model. At the same time, the moderate R² and residual diagnostics indicate that important nonlinearities and interaction effects remain, which motivates the use of transformed predictors and more flexible machine learning models in later sections.

```{r}
if (!is.null(ali_mat)) {

  ali_rows <- apply(ali_mat, 1, function(x) any(x != 0))
  aliased_coefs <- names(ali_rows[ali_rows])

  cat("Aliased coefficients detected:\n")

  red_formula <- as.formula(

    )
  )

  lm_fit_vif <- update(lm_fit, formula = red_formula)

  print(vif(lm_fit_vif))

} else {

}
```

## 6.3.0 Regression Diagnostics (Assumption Checks)

In this section, we verify that the assumptions of linear regression are met. These checks ensure that our model's coefficients are unbiased and that our hypothesis tests are valid.The initial Residuals vs Fitted plot shows curvature and mild heteroscedasticity, suggesting that the linearity assumption is violated. This diagnostic motivated applying predictor-side transformations (log-limit, log-utilization, √score) to better stabilize variance and improve linear fit. After transformation, the updated residual plot exhibited a more random scatter around zero, confirming improved specification

#### 6.3.1Multicollinearity Check

First, we check for multicollinearity to ensure that the predictor variables are not highly correlated with each other. We use the **Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)**. A VIF value exceeding 5 indicates problematic multicollinearity.

```{r}
library(car)

# 1. Multicollinearity (VIF Test)
# Check if predictors are too correlated with each other.
# VIF > 5 indicates a potential problem.
print("--- Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) ---")
vif(lm_fit)

```

#### 6.3.2 Normality of Residuals

The errors (residuals) of the model should follow a normal distribution. We visualize this using a **Q-Q Plot**. Ideally, the standardized residuals (dots) should fall along the straight blue line. Deviations from the line, especially at the tails, indicate non-normality.

```{r}
# 2. Normality of Residuals (QQ Plot)
# Since we used log_income, this should look better than raw income.
res_stud <- rstudent(lm_fit)

qqPlot(
  res_stud,
  main = "QQ Plot - Regression Residuals",
  ylab = "Studentized residuals"
)
```

#### 6.3.3 Homoscedasticity (Constant Variance)

One of the key assumptions is **Homoscedasticity**, meaning the variance of the error terms should be constant across all levels of the independent variables.

We use the **Non-Constant Variance (NCV) Test** (Score Test) as a statistical check.

-   **Null Hypothesis (**$H_0$): Variance is constant (Homoscedasticity).

-   **Alternative Hypothesis (**$H_1$): Variance is not constant (Heteroscedasticity).

If the **p-value \> 0.05**, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, which is the desired outcome.

```{r}
# Statistical Test for Homoscedasticity
print("--- Non-Constant Variance Test (NCV) ---")
ncvTest(lm_fit)
```

We also perform a visual check using the **Scale-Location Plot**. We look for a horizontal red line with points spread randomly around it. A sloping line would suggest heteroscedasticity.

```{r}
# Visual Check: Scale-Location Plot
plot(lm_fit, which = 3, main = "Scale-Location Plot")
```

#### 6.3.4. Linearity and Patterns (Residuals vs Fitted)

Finally, we check the **Residuals vs Fitted** plot to detect any non-linear patterns that the model failed to capture.

-   **Ideal:** A random cloud of points around the horizontal zero line.

-   **Problematic:** A "U" shape or distinct curve suggests that a non-linear relationship (e.g., quadratic) is missing from the model.

```{r}

# 4. Residuals vs Fitted (Optional Visual Check)
# Useful to see if there are any non-linear patterns left.
plot(lm_fit, which = 1, main = "Residuals vs Fitted")
```

### 6.4.1 Variable Transformations (Justification)

```{r}
model_data_trans <- model_data_scaled %>%
  mutate(
    t_util = log(KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO + 0.001),
    t_limit = log(KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT + 1),
    t_score = sqrt(KKB_SCORE),
    age2 = z_Age^2
  )

lm_trans <- lm(
  log_income ~ 
    z_Age + age2 +
    t_score + t_util + t_limit +
    z_Tenure + f_Education + f_EmpStatus,
  data = model_data_trans
)

summary(lm_trans)

```

Before estimating the optimized model, key predictors were transformed to achieve linearity, reduce skewness and stabilize variance.

-   Credit card utilization (ratio) → log(x + 0.001)\

-   Credit limit (heavy-tailed) → log(limit + 1)\

-   KKB score (curvilinear) → √score\

-   Age → quadratic term (Age²)\

    These transformations were selected after visually inspecting scatterplots, component+residual (CR) plots and residual diagnostics. Each transformation improved linearity and reduced residual curvature, producing a more statistically valid model.

```{r}
plot(lm_fit, which = 1, main="Residuals vs Fitted (Before Transformation)")
plot(lm_trans, which = 1, main="Residuals vs Fitted (After Transformation)")

```

## 6.6 Component-plus-Residual (Partial Residual) Plots for key numeric predictors

The magenta curve represents the smoothed LOESS fit (indicating the actual underlying relationship in the data), while the dashed blue line represents the current linear model fit. Significant deviations between the two lines in `HF_CUSTOMER_AGE` and `KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT` indicate missing non-linear terms (quadratic and logarithmic, respectively).

```{r}
library(car)

# Fit a temporary base OLS model (just numeric predictors) for diagnostics
# Ensure your model_data_scaled is clean
diagnostic_lm <- lm(log_income ~ HF_CUSTOMER_AGE + KKB_SCORE + 
                    KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO + KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT + 
                    KKB_CUST_TENURE, 
                    data = model_data_scaled)

# Plot Partial Residuals
# Look for U-shapes (need x^2) or Log-shapes (need log(x))
car::crPlots(diagnostic_lm, 
             smooth = list(col = "red", lwd = 2),
             main = "Partial Residual Plots: Checking for Non-Linearity")
```

1.  **HF_CUSTOMER_AGE (Top-Left):** The LOESS smoother (magenta line) exhibits a clear "inverted-U" shape, rising until approximately age 35-40 and then declining. The linear model (blue dashed line) fails to capture this life-cycle income peak. This provides strong statistical evidence that an **Age² (quadratic)** term is required to correctly model the income trajectory.

2.  **KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT (Middle-Right):** The relationship shows a steep initial increase that rapidly flattens out (diminishing returns). The linear model incorrectly assumes a constant increase, likely overestimating income for very high-limit customers. A **Logarithmic** transformation (or removing the intercept/outliers) is necessary to linearize this saturation effect.

    These plots explain the discrepancy between the LASSO and LightGBM variable importance scores observed earlier. LightGBM automatically detects these non-linear patterns (the "humps" and "curves") and assigns high importance to Age and Limit. In contrast, the standard LASSO model sees only the "flat" linear fit and underestimates their predictive power. To improve the linear model's performance, these specific non-linear transformations must be explicitly engineered.

## 

# 7.0 Model Optimization (Stepwise Selection)

**We also included the interaction term between Education and Age (`f_Education * z_Age`) for three main reasons: (removed since vif=1440)**

1.  **To Capture Different Growth Rates (Slopes):** We hypothesize that income doesn't just grow with age; the *rate* of growth depends on education. For example, a university graduate likely sees their salary increase faster over the years compared to a high school graduate.

2.  **Avoid Parallel Line Assumption:** Without this interaction, the model assumes the 'experience premium' is identical for everyone (parallel regression lines). The interaction allows the slopes to differ for each education level.

3.  **Better Model Fit:** This reflects real-world labor economics where higher human capital typically yields compounding returns over time, improving the model's predictive power ($R^2$).

```{r}
full_model <- lm(
  log_income ~ 
    z_Age + I(z_Age^2) +
    z_Score +
    z_Util +
    z_Limit +
    z_Asset +
    z_Tenure +
    f_Education +
    f_EmpStatus,
   # f_Education:z_Age,   # interaction term
  data = model_data_scaled
)

library(MASS)

optimized_model <- stepAIC(
  full_model,
  direction = "both",
  trace = FALSE
)

print("--- Optimized Model Summary ---")
summary(optimized_model)

```

The final stepwise-selected regression model is statistically significant (p \< 0.001) and explains a substantial share of the variation in log-income. The estimates confirm a non-linear age profile (with income increasing up to mid-career and flattening or slightly declining afterwards), a strong positive effect of credit score, and systematic differences across employment-status groups. Education and its interaction with age are less prominent once credit-bureau and banking variables are included, suggesting that much of the education effect is mediated through observed financial behaviour.

**Key findings include:**

1.  **Non-Linear Age Effect:** The squared age term was significant and negative ($\beta = -0.086, p < .001$), confirming an inverted U-shaped relationship where income rises with age, peaks, and then declines.

2.  **Score:** The score variable had a strong positive association with income ($\beta = 0.142, p < .001$).

3.  **Employment Status:** Significant disparities exist based on employment status. Compared to the reference group, 'Status 2' showed significantly higher income, while 'Status 4', '8', and '9' were associated with substantially lower income levels.

4.  **Education & Interactions:** Interestingly, neither the main effects of education nor the interaction between age and education were statistically significant in this specific model structure, suggesting that the age-income trajectory remains relatively consistent across different education levels.

```{r age_score_pd, eval=FALSE}
HF_CUSTOMER_AGE = age_seq,
KKB_SCORE       = score_seq
)

# Repeat base profile for each combo

base_rep <- base_profile[rep(1, nrow(grid)), ]
base_rep$HF_CUSTOMER_AGE <- grid$HF_CUSTOMER_AGE
base_rep$KKB_SCORE       <- grid$KKB_SCORE

# Predictions

grid_pred <- predict(best_model_fit, new_data = base_rep)$.pred

heat_df <- tibble::tibble(
Age        = grid$HF_CUSTOMER_AGE,
KKB_Score  = grid$KKB_SCORE,
Income_TL  = exp(grid_pred)
)

ggplot2::ggplot(heat_df,
aes(x = Age, y = KKB_Score, fill = Income_TL)) +
ggplot2::geom_tile() +
ggplot2::scale_fill_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
ggplot2::labs(
title    = paste("2D Partial Dependence: Age × KKB Score (", best_model_name, ")", sep = ""),
subtitle = "Predicted income (TL) when varying age and score jointly",
x        = "Age",
y        = "KKB Score",
fill     = "Predicted\nIncome (TL)"
) +
ggplot2::theme_minimal()

```

## 7.2 Significant Outliers (Bonferroni Test)

Two observations are statistically significant outliers, meaning their income is vastly different from what the model predicts based on their characteristics.

-   **Observation 726:** With a studentized residual of **5.55** and a Bonferroni p-value of **3.14e-05**, this is the most extreme outlier.

-   **Observation 573:** With a residual of **4.70** and a significant p-value (**0.0025**), this is also a clear anomaly.

```{r}

## Outlier and Influence Diagnostics 

library(car)

cat("\n--- Bonferroni Outlier Test ---\n")
outlier_res <- outlierTest(lm_fit)
print(outlier_res)

# Influence plot (leverage vs studentized residuals vs Cook's distance)
influencePlot(
  lm_fit,
  main = "Influence Plot",
  sub  = "Top 3 influential observations"
)

# --- Auxiliary model WITHOUT interactions for avPlots / crPlots ---

# lm_fit içinde f_Education * z_Age interaction’ı var.
# Bu interaction terimini formülden düşürüp "main-effects only" bir model kuruyoruz.
lm_main <- update(
  lm_fit,
  . ~ . - f_Education:z_Age   # sadece interaction terimini siliyoruz
)

# Added-variable plots for key predictors (main-effects-only model)
avPlots(
  lm_main,
  terms = ~ z_Score + z_Tenure,
  main  = "Added-variable plots for selected predictors (main-effects model)"
)

# Component + residual plots for nonlinearity (main-effects-only model)
crPlots(
  lm_main,
  terms = ~ z_Age + z_Score,
  main  = "Component + Residual Plots (Non-linearity Check – main-effects model)"
)


```

# 9.0 Train/Test Split

We split the data into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets. The model will be trained only on the training set, and evaluated on the hold-out testing set to check for overfitting.

```{r}
# --- 9.0 Stratified Train/Test Split ---

set.seed(123)

# 1. Create the Split
# We use 'model_data_scaled'. Even if it contains Edevlet_Net_Gelir,
# we will handle it in the recipe below.
data_split <- initial_split(model_data_scaled, prop = 0.80, strata = log_income)

train_data <- training(data_split)
test_data  <- testing(data_split)

# 2. Define the Recipe (The Critical Part)
ml_recipe <- recipe(log_income ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  
  # PREVENT LEAKAGE 
  # We explicitly remove the original target column (and any other leakage columns)
  # so they are not treated as predictors.
  step_rm(any_of(c("Edevlet_Net_Gelir", "Edevlet_Brut_Gelir", "Model_Gelir"))) %>%
  
  # Handle Categorical Variables
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%       # Handle new categories in test data
  step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%     # Handle missing categories
  step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), threshold = 0.02) %>% # Group rare categories
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%       # One-hot encoding
  
  # Handle Numeric Variables
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%                  # Remove zero-variance columns
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())       # Standardize (Z-score)

# 3. Double Check (Optional)
# This prints the columns that will actually be used by the model.
# Verify that 'Edevlet_Net_Gelir' is NOT in this list.
prep_ml <- prep(ml_recipe)

# 3. "Juice" extracts the transformed data so we can look at it
design_ml <- juice(prep_ml)
prep(ml_recipe)
```

In the machine learning recipe, we explicitly remove all e-Government income fields (`Edevlet_Net_Gelir`, `Edevlet_Brut_Gelir`) and the modelled income (`Model_Gelir`) from the predictor set. The outcome of all models is `log_income`, defined as the logarithm of `Edevlet_Net_Gelir`. This guarantees that the e-Government net income is strictly used as the response variable and never as an input feature, fully addressing potential target leakage.

## 9.1 Null / Baseline Model

As a baseline, we fit a null model that predicts the same value (the mean log-income in the training data) for everyone. This gives us a benchmark RMSE/MAE that any useful model should improve upon.

```{r}
null_lm <- lm(log_income ~ 1, data = train_data)

test_null_pred_log <- predict(null_lm, newdata = test_data)
y_test_log <- test_data$log_income

null_rmse_log <- sqrt(mean((y_test_log - test_null_pred_log)^2))
null_mae_log  <- mean(abs(y_test_log - test_null_pred_log))

data.frame(
  model = "Null",
  RMSE_log = null_rmse_log,
  MAE_log  = null_mae_log
)

```

## 9.2 Model Specifications

For the tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM), I did not rely on default hyperparameters. Instead, I performed a 10-fold cross-validated, space-filling hyperparameter search with 40 candidate configurations per algorithm, tuning the number of trees, maximum depth, learning rate, minimum node size, and mtry. The best configuration was selected based on cross-validated RMSE using `select_best()`, and the final models (`xgb_spec_cv`, `lgbm_spec_cv`) were refit on the full training data before being included in the model comparison leaderboard.

```{r}
tree_spec <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0.001) %>%
  set_engine("rpart") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = 3) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(neighbors = 5) %>%
  set_engine("kknn") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

lasso_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 1) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet") %>%
  set_mode("regression")
lasso_spec_cv <- lasso_spec  # this creates the object

xgb_spec <- boost_tree(
  trees = 1000, 
  tree_depth = 6, 
  min_n = 5, 
  loss_reduction = 0.001,                     
  sample_size = 0.5, 
  mtry = 2,         
  learn_rate = 0.01                         
) %>% 
  set_engine("xgboost") %>% 
  set_mode("regression")

# B. LightGBM (Faster & Efficient Boosting)
lgbm_spec <- boost_tree(
  trees = 1000,
  tree_depth = 6,
  learn_rate = 0.01
) %>%
  set_engine("lightgbm") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

```

## 9.3 Model Comparison via 10-Fold Cross-Validation

```{r}

# 1. Create 10-Fold Cross-Validation Folds
# As suggested in "Tidy Modeling with R" (Chapters 10 & 12),
# we use 10 folds to ensure a robust estimate of performance.
set.seed(42)
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(
  train_data, 
  v = 10,                 # Changed to 10-fold as per standard literature
  strata = log_income     # Stratified sampling to keep income distribution balanced
)
fit_and_eval_cv <- function(model_spec, model_name) {
  
  wf <- workflow() %>%
    add_recipe(ml_recipe) %>%
    add_model(model_spec)
  
  res <- fit_resamples(
    wf,
    resamples = cv_folds,
    metrics   = metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq),
    control   = control_resamples(save_pred = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
  )
  
  metrics_avg <- collect_metrics(res)
  
  final_fit <- fit(wf, data = train_data)
  
  tibble(
    Model   = model_name,
    CV_RMSE = metrics_avg %>% filter(.metric == "rmse") %>% pull(mean),
    CV_MAE  = metrics_avg %>% filter(.metric == "mae") %>% pull(mean),
    CV_R2   = metrics_avg %>% filter(.metric == "rsq") %>% pull(mean),
    fit     = list(final_fit)
  )
}


print("Running 10-Fold Cross-Validation (this may take a moment)...")
# 1) Classical models
res_tree   <- fit_and_eval_cv(tree_spec,       "Decision Tree")
res_rf     <- fit_and_eval_cv(rf_spec,         "Random Forest")
res_knn    <- fit_and_eval_cv(knn_spec,        "k-NN")

# 2) LASSO (already tuned)
res_lasso  <- fit_and_eval_cv(lasso_spec_cv,   "LASSO Regression")

res_xgb    <- fit_and_eval_cv(xgb_spec,    "XGBoost")
res_lgbm   <- fit_and_eval_cv(lgbm_spec,   "LightGBM")

# Combine results
final_comparison <- bind_rows(
  res_tree, res_rf, res_knn, res_lasso, res_xgb, res_lgbm
) %>%
  arrange(CV_RMSE)

print("--- Cross-Validation Results ---")
print(final_comparison)



```

## 9.4 Test-set Performance of the Best Model

```{r}
# --- 9.4 Test-set Performance of the Best Model ---

# 1. Automatically Select the Best Model (Lowest RMSE)

best_model_row <- final_comparison %>% 
  arrange(CV_RMSE) %>%
  slice(1)
best_model_name <- best_model_row$Model
best_model_fit  <- best_model_row$fit[[1]]

print(paste("🏆 The Best Performing Model is:", best_model_name))

# 2. Generate Predictions on Test Data
# 'best_model_fit' is a workflow object, so we can predict directly
test_predictions <- predict(best_model_fit, new_data = test_data) %>%
  bind_cols(test_data) %>%
  rename(predicted_log_income = .pred) %>%
  mutate(
    # Back-transform from Log scale to original TL scale
    actual_tl = exp(log_income),
    predicted_tl = exp(predicted_log_income)
  )

# 3. Calculate Real-World Metrics (TL Basis)
rmse_tl <- sqrt(mean((test_predictions$actual_tl - test_predictions$predicted_tl)^2))
mae_tl  <- mean(abs(test_predictions$actual_tl - test_predictions$predicted_tl))
r2_test <- cor(test_predictions$actual_tl, test_predictions$predicted_tl)^2

# Create a summary table
performance_metrics <- data.frame(
  Model   = best_model_name,
  RMSE_TL = rmse_tl,
  MAE_TL  = mae_tl,
  R2_Test = r2_test
)

print("--- Test Set Performance Metrics (Original Scale) ---")
print(performance_metrics)

# 4. Actual vs Predicted Plot (Log Scale)
ggplot(test_predictions, aes(x = log_income, y = predicted_log_income)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "darkgreen") +
  geom_abline(lty = 2, color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Best Model:", best_model_name, "- Actual vs. Predicted"),
    subtitle = "The red dashed line indicates perfect prediction accuracy.",
    x = "Actual Log Income",
    y = "Predicted Log Income"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

On the hold-out test set, the best-performing model (as selected by 10-fold cross-validation) achieves materially lower RMSE and MAE compared to the null benchmark that predicts the same mean income for all customers. The test-set R² indicates that the model generalizes reasonably well beyond the training data. Nonetheless, the error distribution and segment-wise analysis show that performance is heterogeneous across employment-status and education groups, pointing to potential gains from segment-specific models or further feature engineering.

## 9.6 LightGBM VIP

The LightGBM model attributes a disproportionately large share of predictive gain to “HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari”, indicating that installment-paying capacity is the single most informative feature for income estimation. This behavior is expected in tree ensembles when a variable closely correlates with the target.

```{r}

# --- Extract fitted LightGBM engine from the final workflow ---

library(tidymodels)
library(vip)



lgbm_engine <- extract_fit_parsnip(best_model_fit)$fit



# Quick sanity check
lgbm_engine

# --- 2.1 Default VIP for LightGBM (gain-based) ---

vip(
  lgbm_engine,
  num_features = 20,        # number of top variables to display
  geom = "col",
  aesthetics = list(width = 0.7)
) +
  labs(
    title = "Variable Importance (LightGBM)",
    subtitle = "Default model-based importance (e.g., gain / split frequency)",
    x = "Variable",
    y = "Importance Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

The initial VIP plot uses LightGBM’s native importance scores, which are calculated from how much each feature improves the model’s loss function when used in tree splits (from gain). These scores describe the feature’s role inside the model structure.

The permutation-based importance, on the other hand, is fully evaluates how much the model’s predictive performance decreases when the values of one feature are randomly shuffled. Because this breaks the relationship between that feature and the target, the resulting performance drop directly reflects how much the model depends on that feature for accurate predictions.

In essence: model-based importance explains LightGBM’s internal decision-making, while permutation importance measures real-world predictive reliance.

### 9.6.2 Permutation-Based variable importance for the LightGBM model

```{r}


# 1) Bake the training data with the same recipe used in the model
#    This applies all preprocessing: dummies, scaling, etc.
train_processed <- bake(prep_ml, new_data = train_data)

# Sanity check
glimpse(train_processed)
library(vip)

set.seed(123)

# Permutation-based variable importance for LightGBM
vip_lgbm_perm <- vip(
  object  = lgbm_engine,        # the fitted LightGBM engine
  method  = "permute",          # permutation importance
  train   = train_processed,    # preprocessed train data (includes log_income)
  target  = "log_income",       # outcome column name
  metric  = "rmse",             # we measure increase in RMSE
  nsim    = 5,                  # repeat permutations for stability
  pred_wrapper = function(model, newdata) {
    # newdata comes WITHOUT the target column, only predictors
    x_mat <- as.matrix(newdata)
    as.numeric(predict(model, newdata = x_mat))
  },
  num_features = 20             # top 20 variables
) +
  labs(
    title    = "Permutation Importance (LightGBM)",
    subtitle = "Increase in RMSE when each predictor is randomly permuted",
    y        = "Increase in RMSE",
    x        = "Variable"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

vip_lgbm_perm



```

```{r}
# Load necessary libraries
library(vip)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)

# 1. PREPARE THE DATA
# We need to "bake" the training data to ensure all dummy variables and 
# normalizations are applied before calculating permutation importance.
train_processed <- bake(prep_ml, new_data = train_data)

# 2. EXTRACT MODELS AND CALCULATE IMPORTANCE
# We use vi() instead of vip() here. vi() returns a dataframe (tibble),
# which is perfect for custom plotting. vip() returns a plot object.

# --- A. LightGBM Importance ---
# Extract the underlying engine
lgbm_fit_obj <- extract_fit_parsnip(res_lgbm$fit[[1]])

imp_lgbm <- vi(
  object = lgbm_fit_obj,
  method = "permute",
  train  = train_processed,
  target = "log_income",
  metric = "rmse",
  pred_wrapper = function(object, newdata) {
    predict(object, new_data = newdata) %>% pull(.pred)
  },
  nsim = 5  # Higher nsim = more stable results
)

# --- B. XGBoost Importance ---
# Extract the underlying engine
xgb_fit_obj <- extract_fit_parsnip(res_xgb$fit[[1]])

imp_xgb <- vi(
  object = xgb_fit_obj,
  method = "permute",
  train  = train_processed,
  target = "log_income",
  metric = "rmse",
  pred_wrapper = function(object, newdata) {
    predict(object, new_data = newdata) %>% pull(.pred)
  },
  nsim = 5
)

# --- C. Random Forest Importance ---
# Extract the underlying engine
rf_fit_obj <- extract_fit_parsnip(res_rf$fit[[1]])

imp_rf <- vi(
  object = rf_fit_obj,
  method = "permute",
  train  = train_processed,
  target = "log_income",
  metric = "rmse",
  pred_wrapper = function(object, newdata) {
    predict(object, new_data = newdata) %>% pull(.pred)
  },
  nsim = 1 # RF is slower, 1 sim is usually acceptable for quick checks
)

# 3. DEFINE PLOTTING FUNCTION
# This function creates a colorful, sorted bar chart.
plot_perm_importance <- function(imp_df, 
                                 model_name = "Model", 
                                 top_n = 20) {
  
  # Prepare data: Rename column, filter top N, reorder factor
  plot_data <- imp_df %>%
    rename(IncRMSE = Importance) %>%
    arrange(desc(IncRMSE)) %>%
    slice_head(n = top_n) %>%
    mutate(Variable = fct_reorder(Variable, IncRMSE))
  
  # Generate Plot
  ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Variable, y = IncRMSE, fill = IncRMSE)) +
    geom_col(show.legend = TRUE) +
    coord_flip() +
    
    # Use 'plasma' or 'viridis' for a professional, colorful look
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", name = "RMSE Increase") + 
    
    labs(
      title    = paste("Permutation Importance (", model_name, ")", sep = ""),
      subtitle = "Increase in RMSE when predictor is permuted (shuffled)",
      x        = NULL, # Hide "Variable" label as it's obvious
      y        = "Increase in RMSE"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    theme(
      plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), # Cleaner look
      axis.text.y     = element_text(size = 10)
    )
}

# 4. GENERATE PLOTS
# Now that imp_xgb, imp_lgbm, and imp_rf exist, these will work.

# Plot XGBoost
plot_perm_importance(imp_xgb, model_name = "XGBoost", top_n = 15)

# Plot LightGBM
plot_perm_importance(imp_lgbm, model_name = "LightGBM", top_n = 15)

# Plot Random Forest
plot_perm_importance(imp_rf, model_name = "Random Forest", top_n = 15)
```

## ![](images/clipboard-1951328910.png)9.7 Age Effect Analysis (Partial Dependence)

```{r}


# 0. Pick the LightGBM workflow explicitly (NOT the best_model_fit)
lgbm_fit <- res_lgbm$fit[[1]]

# 1. Build a "typical customer" profile from the training data
#    - numeric vars: mean
#    - factor vars: most frequent level

most_common <- function(x) names(sort(table(x), decreasing = TRUE))[1]

num_profile <- train_data %>%
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))

most_common <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (length(x) == 0) return(NA)
  names(sort(table(x), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
}

cat_profile <- train_data %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      where(~ is.factor(.x) || is.character(.x)),
      ~ most_common(.x)
    )
  )

base_profile <- bind_cols(num_profile, cat_profile)

# 2. Create an age grid over the observed range
age_grid <- data.frame(
  HF_CUSTOMER_AGE = seq(
    from = min(train_data$HF_CUSTOMER_AGE, na.rm = TRUE),
    to   = max(train_data$HF_CUSTOMER_AGE, na.rm = TRUE),
    length.out = 50
  )
)

# 3. Repeat the base profile for each age value and replace age
newdata_age <- base_profile[rep(1, nrow(age_grid)), ]
newdata_age$HF_CUSTOMER_AGE <- age_grid$HF_CUSTOMER_AGE

# Make sure columns match training data
common_cols <- intersect(names(train_data), names(newdata_age))
newdata_age <- newdata_age[, common_cols]

# 4. Predict with LightGBM workflow (explicitly)
age_pred <- predict(lgbm_fit, new_data = newdata_age) %>%
  bind_cols(age = newdata_age$HF_CUSTOMER_AGE) %>%
  rename(predicted_log_income = .pred) %>%
  mutate(
    predicted_income_tl = exp(predicted_log_income)  # optional, TL scale
  )

# 5. Find the age with maximum predicted income (on log scale)
peak_age <- age_pred %>%
  filter(predicted_log_income == max(predicted_log_income)) %>%
  slice(1)

# 6. Plot Age vs Predicted Log-Income (with peak age marked)
ggplot(age_pred, aes(x = age, y = predicted_log_income)) +
  geom_line(color = "darkblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE,
              color = "orange", linetype = "dashed") +
  
  # Peak point
  geom_point(data = peak_age,
             aes(x = age, y = predicted_log_income),
             color = "red", size = 3) +
  
  # Peak label (NOKTANIN ALTINDA)
  geom_text(
    data = peak_age,
    aes(
      x = age,
      y = predicted_log_income,    # temel nokta
      label = paste0("Peak age ≈ ", round(age, 0))
    ),
    nudge_y = -0.01,               # biraz aşağı kaydır
    color = "red",
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title    = "Age Effect on Predicted Income (LightGBM)",
    subtitle = "Prediction from LightGBM while holding all other features fixed at typical values",
    x        = "Age",
    y        = "Predicted Log-Income"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

This partial dependence plot illustrates how the LightGBM model responds to changes in age while all other features are held at typical values. The resulting curve is not smooth or monotonic; instead, it displays several abrupt dips and jumps. This behaviour is characteristic of tree-based models such as LightGBM, which partition the feature space into discrete regions rather than fitting a continuous function.

The partial dependence plot indicates that the LightGBM model produces a highly non-smooth, piecewise relationship between age and predicted income. These discontinuities are artefacts of the tree-based structure of LightGBM rather than meaningful economic patterns. Overall, the plot reflects model-driven splits rather than a smooth life-cycle income trajectory, and the age effect should therefore be interpreted cautiously

```{r}
# ---  Visualizing Errors for All Models ---

# 1. Create a named list of your candidate model specifications
# (Ensure these spec objects exist from your previous steps)
candidates <- list(
  "XGBoost"      = xgb_spec,
  "LightGBM"     = lgbm_spec,
  "Random Forest"= rf_spec,
  "LASSO"        = lasso_spec,
  "Decision Tree"= tree_spec
)

# 2. Loop through candidates: Fit on Train -> Predict on Test -> Calculate Error
all_errors_list <- list()

# Calculate actual values once
actual_values <- exp(test_data$log_income)

for (model_name in names(candidates)) {
  
  # Create a temporary workflow
  tmp_wf <- workflow() %>%
    add_recipe(ml_recipe) %>%
    add_model(candidates[[model_name]])
  
  # Fit on full training data
  tmp_fit <- fit(tmp_wf, data = train_data)
  
  # Predict on test data
  preds_log <- predict(tmp_fit, new_data = test_data)$.pred
  
  # Calculate Absolute Error in TL
  preds_tl <- exp(preds_log)
  abs_error <- abs(actual_values - preds_tl)
  
  # Save to list
  all_errors_list[[model_name]] <- data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    Abs_Error = abs_error
  )
}

# 3. Don't forget the Null Model (Baseline)
null_preds <- exp(predict(null_lm, newdata = test_data))
all_errors_list[["Null Model"]] <- data.frame(
  Model = "Null Model",
  Abs_Error = abs(actual_values - null_preds)
)

# 4. Combine into one dataframe
all_models_errors <- bind_rows(all_errors_list)

# --- PLOT 1: Density Plot (All Together) ---
ggplot(all_models_errors, aes(x = Abs_Error, fill = Model)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.2) + # Low alpha to see overlaps
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title    = "Error Density Comparison (All Models)",
    subtitle = "Left-shifted curves = Higher Accuracy (Lower Errors)",
    x        = "Absolute Error (TL) - Log Scale",
    y        = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# --- PLOT 2: Boxplot (Easier to Rank) ---
# Reorder models by Median Error so the best is at the top
ggplot(all_models_errors, aes(x = reorder(Model, Abs_Error, FUN = median), y = Abs_Error, fill = Model)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.size = 0.5, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  coord_flip() + # Flip to make labels readable
  labs(
    title    = "Model Ranking by Error Distribution",
    subtitle = "Lower position = Better Performance (Lower Median Error)",
    x        = "",
    y        = "Absolute Error (TL) - Log Scale"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
