# 10.1 LASSO Hyperparameter Tuning

```{r}
# 1. Define a tunable specification
lasso_tune_spec <- linear_reg(
  penalty = tune(), 
  mixture = 1         
) %>% 
  set_engine("glmnet") %>% 
  set_mode("regression")

# 2. Create a grid of 50 possible lambda values
lambda_grid <- grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-5, -1)), levels = 50)

# 3. Create workflow
lasso_tune_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(lasso_rec) %>%       
  add_model(lasso_tune_spec)

# 4. Run Tuning (using the existing cv_folds from Step 9.3)
doParallel::registerDoParallel() # Optional: Speed up if you have multiple cores

lasso_grid_results <- tune_grid(
  lasso_tune_wf,
  resamples = cv_folds,
  grid      = lambda_grid,
  metrics   = metric_set(rmse, rsq)
)

# 5. Visualize the Tuning Results
lasso_grid_results %>%
  collect_metrics() %>%
  filter(.metric == "rmse") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = penalty, y = mean)) +
  geom_line(size = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(color = "darkblue") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "LASSO Tuning: RMSE vs. Penalty (Lambda)",
    subtitle = "Finding the 'Sweet Spot' where error is minimized",
    x = "Penalty (Lambda) - Log Scale",
    y = "Mean RMSE (Cross-Validation)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Coefficient path plot shows that only a limited subset of predictors remains non-zero as λ increases. This indicates that the dataset contains many weak or redundant variables, and LASSO effectively shrinks them toward zero, retaining only a small set of strong predictors.

## 10.2 LASSO Trace Plot (Variable Selection Path)

Optimal λ is very small, meaning strong regularization hurts performance in this dataset. The model needs many predictors to preserve accuracy, and aggressive shrinkage causes underfitting.

```{r}


lasso_prep <- prep(lasso_rec, training = model_data_scaled)
design_lasso <- juice(lasso_prep)

# 2) X ve y'yi oluştur
X_train_mat <- as.matrix(dplyr::select(design_lasso, -log_income))
y_train_vec <- design_lasso$log_income
# 1) Extract full coefficient matrix from glmnet
glmnet_fit <- glmnet(X_train_mat, y_train_vec, alpha = 1)
coef_full <- as.matrix(glmnet_fit$beta)

# 2) Identify variables that are ever non-zero across the lambda path
nonzero_rows <- rowSums(abs(coef_full) > 0) > 0

coef_nonzero <- coef_full[nonzero_rows, , drop = FALSE]

# 3) Rank variables by maximum absolute coefficient size
row_max <- apply(abs(coef_nonzero), 1, max)
top_idx <- order(row_max, decreasing = TRUE)

# Select the top 15 (or fewer if less exist)
k <- min(15, length(top_idx))
coef_mat <- coef_nonzero[top_idx[1:k], , drop = FALSE]

# 4) Plot coefficient paths clearly
matplot(
  x    = -log(glmnet_fit$lambda),
  y    = t(coef_mat),
  type = "l",
  lty  = 1,
  lwd  = 2,
  col  = rainbow(nrow(coef_mat)),
  xlab = "-Log(lambda)",
  ylab = "Coefficient",
  main = "LASSO Coefficient Paths – Top Variables Only"
)

legend(
  "topleft",
  legend = rownames(coef_mat),
  col    = rainbow(nrow(coef_mat)),
  lty    = 1,
  cex    = 0.65,
  bty    = "n"
)


```

**Figure displays the LASSO coefficient paths for the most influential predictors in the model.** Each colored line represents how a variable’s coefficient changes as the regularization penalty λ increases (moving right on the x-axis). As λ becomes larger, LASSO shrinks most coefficients toward zero, while only a small subset of predictors maintain non-zero values.

The variables that remain active over a wide range of λ particularly several education dummies, employment-status categories, credit tenure, credit score, and age-group indicators—are the predictors with the strongest and most stable association with log-income.This pattern shows that LASSO actively performs variable selection: weak or redundant predictors rapidly collapse to zero, whereas high-signal predictors persist. The resulting model is therefore more interpretable and robust, retaining only the variables that meaningfully contribute to income prediction.

## 10.3 Select Best vs. Simplest (1-SE Rule)

```{r}


# Get the absolute best lambda
best_rmse <- select_best(lasso_grid_results, metric = "rmse")

# Get the simplest lambda within 1 standard error of the best
best_1se  <- select_by_one_std_err(lasso_grid_results, metric = "rmse", desc(penalty))

print(paste("Best Lambda (Lowest Error):", round(best_rmse$penalty, 5)))
print(paste("1-SE Lambda (Simplest Model):", round(best_1se$penalty, 5)))

# Update workflow with the Best Lambda and finalize
final_lasso_wf <- finalize_workflow(lasso_tune_wf, best_rmse)
final_lasso_fit <- fit(final_lasso_wf, data = train_data)

# Extract and plot the coefficients of the OPTIMIZED model
final_lasso_fit %>%
  extract_fit_parsnip() %>%
  vip(num_features = 20, geom = "point",
      aesthetics = list(color = "darkred", size = 3)) +
  labs(
    title = "Variable Importance (Optimized LASSO)",
    subtitle = "t_PaymentCap = log(HF_Odeyebilecegi_Taksit_Tutari + 1):\nA log-transformed payment capacity measure capturing non-linear effects",
    x = "Importance",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


```

**Figure "Variable Importance (Optimized LASSO)"** presents the same information in a more interpretable way using a variable-importance representation. Instead of plotting the raw β’s, the `vip` function ranks predictors by the absolute size of their standardized coefficients and omits the intercept. Education-related dummies, employment-status categories, credit-tenure, and credit score emerge as the most influential drivers of log-income. This plot therefore highlights which variables matter most for prediction, while the coefficient plot shows how (positive/negative) they affect income.

**Figure "Coefficient Magnitudes at Optimal λ"** reports the raw coefficient estimates of the optimized LASSO model. The intercept is close to 10, reflecting the average log-income in the sample, while all slope coefficients are much smaller in magnitude. Coefficients to the right of zero indicate variables that increase predicted income, whereas negative coefficients reduce it.

The heatmap shows how variable coefficients evolve along the LASSO path, with only a few predictors remaining active under strong regularization, confirming their robustness and predictive relevance.

```{r lasso-coef-ggplot, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=15, fig.height=12}

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)
library(stringr)

# 1. Extract glmnet model
glmnet_model <- extract_fit_parsnip(final_lasso_fit)$fit

# 2. Coefficients at optimal lambda (best_rmse$penalty)
coef_mat <- coef(glmnet_model, s = best_rmse$penalty)

# 3. Turn dgCMatrix into a tidy data frame
coef_df <- data.frame(
  term     = rownames(coef_mat),
  estimate = as.numeric(coef_mat)
) %>%
  # remove intercept + zero coefficients
  filter(term != "(Intercept)", estimate != 0) %>%
  # sort by absolute magnitude
  mutate(
    abs_est   = abs(estimate),
    term      = fct_reorder(term, abs_est),
    term_clean = str_wrap(term, width = 22)  # wrap long labels
  ) %>%
  arrange(abs_est)

# 4. Plot – readable, high-res version
ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = estimate, y = term_clean)) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  labs(
    title    = "LASSO Coefficients (λ = Optimal, Intercept Removed)",
    subtitle = "Predictors are standardized → coefficient magnitudes are comparable.",
    x        = "Coefficient value",
    y        = "Predictor"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 18) +
  theme(
    plot.title        = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y       = element_text(size = 12),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )


```

#### Ranking of LASSO-Selected Numeric Predictors by \|t\|-Statistic

```{r lasso-tstats, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=15, fig.height=10}



# -------------------------------------------------------------

# 1) Extract glmnet model and non-zero coefficients

# -------------------------------------------------------------

glmnet_model <- extract_fit_parsnip(final_lasso_fit)$fit

coef_mat <- coef(glmnet_model, s = best_rmse$penalty)

selected_vars_raw <- rownames(coef_mat)[as.numeric(coef_mat) != 0]
selected_vars_raw <- selected_vars_raw[selected_vars_raw != "(Intercept)"]

# -------------------------------------------------------------

# 2) Restrict to numeric, existing, formula-safe predictors

# -------------------------------------------------------------

# (a) Only columns that exist AND are numeric in model_data_scaled

numeric_cols <- names(model_data_scaled)[sapply(model_data_scaled, is.numeric)]

candidate_vars <- intersect(selected_vars_raw, numeric_cols)

# (b) Drop location, tier dummies and factor-style names, and keep formula-safe ones

clean_vars <- candidate_vars %>%
.[!grepl("^İkamet İl", .)] %>%         # drop location dummies if any
.[!grepl("^Tier_", .)] %>%             # drop tier dummies if any
.[!grepl("^f_", .)] %>%                # drop factor-style names if any
.[grepl("^[A-Za-z0-9_\\.]+$", .)]
      # keep only formula-safe names

# Quick check

print(clean_vars)

# If this accidentally becomes empty, stop with a clear message

if (length(clean_vars) == 0) {
stop("No valid numeric LASSO-selected predictors left after cleaning.")
}

# -------------------------------------------------------------

# 3) Build OLS formula using only these numeric predictors

# -------------------------------------------------------------

formula_lasso_ols <- reformulate(
termlabels = clean_vars,
response   = "log_income"
)

print(formula_lasso_ols)

# -------------------------------------------------------------

# 4) Fit OLS model to obtain classical t-statistics

# -------------------------------------------------------------

model_ols <- lm(formula_lasso_ols, data = model_data_scaled)

# -------------------------------------------------------------

# 5) Extract and plot |t-statistics|

# -------------------------------------------------------------

t_df <- tidy(model_ols) %>%
dplyr::filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
dplyr::mutate(
abs_t      = abs(statistic),
term_clean = stringr::str_wrap(term, width = 25)
) %>%

# order by |t| and freeze that order in the factor levels

dplyr::arrange(abs_t) %>%
dplyr::mutate(
term_clean = factor(term_clean, levels = term_clean)
)

ggplot(t_df, aes(x = abs_t, y = term_clean)) +
geom_col(fill = "#E58F65") +
labs(
title    = "Absolute t-statistics from OLS refit on LASSO-selected predictors",
subtitle = "Larger bars indicate stronger marginal significance (in the OLS sense).",
x        = "|t-statistic|",
y        = NULL
) +
theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
theme(
plot.title  = element_text(face = "bold"),
axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11)
)


```

LASSO identifies influential predictors by shrinking coefficients through an ℓ1​ penalty, which prioritizes predictive contribution rather than classical statistical significance.As a result, a variable may receive a non-zero LASSO coefficient even if its marginal linear effect is weak. To assess this difference we refitted an OLS model using only the LASSO-selected predictors and examined the resulting absolute t-statistics (\|t\|).

Overall, the comparison reveals that the strongest LASSO coefficients tend to align with the predictors exhibiting the highest \|t\| values, such as standardized delinquency counts and payment-capacity features.This consistency suggests that LASSO is selecting variables that are not only useful for prediction but also retain statistical relevance in a linear environment.

## 10.4 Feature Importance Comparison: Linear vs Non-Linear

```{r feature-importance-heatmap, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=15, fig.height=8, column="screen-left"}
library(tidymodels)
library(vip)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

extract_vi <- function(model_res) {
  fit <- extract_fit_parsnip(model_res$fit[[1]])
  vi(fit)
}

dt_imp    <- extract_vi(res_tree)   %>% mutate(Model = "Decision Tree")
rf_imp    <- extract_vi(res_rf)     %>% mutate(Model = "Random Forest")
lasso_imp <- extract_vi(res_lasso)  %>% mutate(Model = "LASSO")
xgb_imp   <- extract_vi(res_xgb)    %>% mutate(Model = "XGBoost")
lgbm_imp  <- extract_vi(res_lgbm)   %>% mutate(Model = "LightGBM")

all_imp <- bind_rows(dt_imp, rf_imp, lasso_imp, xgb_imp, lgbm_imp) %>%
  rename(Feature = Variable, Importance = Importance) %>%
  group_by(Model) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = Importance, n = 10) %>%
  mutate(Feature = reorder(Feature, Importance)) %>%
  ungroup()

all_imp$Model <- factor(all_imp$Model,
                        levels = c("Decision Tree", "Random Forest", "LASSO", "XGBoost", "LightGBM"))

model_colors <- c(
  "Decision Tree" = "#F8766D",
  "Random Forest" = "#00BFC4",
  "LASSO"         = "#B79F00",
  "XGBoost"       = "#F564E3",
  "LightGBM"      = "#00BA38"
)

ggplot(all_imp, aes(x = Importance, y = Feature, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ Model, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = model_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Feature Importance Across Different Models",
    subtitle = "Top predictors driving income predictions in each algorithm",
    x = "Importance Score",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 18) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 20),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 13),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

  
```

Figure Comparing which variables drive predictions in each algorithm, compares the top predictors identified by five different algorithms Decision Tree, Random Forest, LASSO, XGBoost, and LightGBM. Despite using fundamentally different modeling paradigms (linear shrinkage vs. tree-based non-linear splits), the models consistently highlight the same core set of variables as the strongest drivers of income: credit score (KKB_SCORE), credit limit (KKB_CC_OPEN_TOT_LIM_AMT), credit tenure (KKB_CUST_TENURE), credit card utilization (KKB_CC_UTIL_RATIO), and age-related features. This convergence across models indicates that these predictors possess a robust, model-independent signal and are structurally important in explaining income.

LASSO additionally prioritizes education- and employment-status dummies because linear models rely more heavily on categorical indicators when capturing structural differences across subgroups. Meanwhile, tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) focus more on numeric credit-behaviour variables because they can naturally exploit non-linear thresholds in these features.

The alignment across models confirms that credit-bureau behavioural variables dominate the predictive structure, while human-capital markers (education, employment status) contribute secondary but consistent effects. The fact that different models never disagree radically strengthens the reliability and stability of the income prediction signal.

```{r feature-importance, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=15, fig.height=8, column="screen-left"}


library(tidymodels)
library(vip)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# ---- 1. Helper: extract raw importance from each fitted model ----
get_vi <- function(model_res, model_name) {
  fit_obj <- extract_fit_parsnip(model_res$fit[[1]])
  vi(fit_obj) %>%
    mutate(Model = model_name)
}

# ---- 2. Stack importance scores from all models ----
vip_all <- bind_rows(
  get_vi(res_tree,  "Decision Tree"),
  get_vi(res_rf,    "Random Forest"),
  get_vi(res_lasso, "LASSO"),
  get_vi(res_xgb,   "XGBoost"),
  get_vi(res_lgbm,  "LightGBM")
)

# ---- 3. Keep globally most important features & rescale within model ----
# 3a) pick top 20 features across all models (by max importance)
top_features <- vip_all %>%
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  summarise(max_imp = max(Importance, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  slice_max(order_by = max_imp, n = 20) %>%
  arrange(desc(max_imp)) %>%
  pull(Variable)

# 3b) filter to those features and rescale to [0,1] within each model
vip_heat <- vip_all %>%
  filter(Variable %in% top_features) %>%
  group_by(Model) %>%
  mutate(RelativeImportance = Importance / max(Importance, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

# 3c) order features for y-axis using global importance
feature_order <- vip_heat %>%
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  summarise(global_imp = max(RelativeImportance, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(global_imp)) %>%
  pull(Variable)

vip_heat <- vip_heat %>%
  mutate(
    Variable = factor(Variable, levels = rev(feature_order)),
    Model = factor(
      Model,
      levels = c("Decision Tree", "Random Forest", "LASSO", "XGBoost", "LightGBM")
    )
  )

# ---- 4. Heatmap plot ----
ggplot(vip_heat, aes(x = Model, y = Variable, fill = RelativeImportance)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Relative importance",
    option = "plasma",
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Feature Importance Across Different Models",
    subtitle = "Importance is rescaled within each model (1 = most important feature)",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 18) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 20),
    plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 14),
    axis.text.x     = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid      = element_blank()
  )


```

# **11. Regional Rent Analysis**

This section investigates how provincial average rent levels (used as a proxy for local cost of living) relate to declared income and educational attainment.

## 11.1 Correlation Between Average Rent and Income

We first compute the correlation between the provincial average rent (`kira_il_ortalama`) and the declared e-government income:

```{r}
cor(df$kira_il_ortalama, df$Edevlet_Net_Gelir,
    use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

```

The correlation is positive, indicating that individuals residing in high-rent regions tend to report higher incomes. This aligns with the expected relationship between cost of living and earning capacity in metropolitan areas.

## 11.2 — Income Distribution Across Rent Quartiles

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

df %>%
  mutate(rent_quartile = ntile(kira_il_ortalama, 4)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(rent_quartile), y = Edevlet_Net_Gelir)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#4A90E2", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Income Distribution Across Rent Quartiles",
    x = "Rent Quartile (1 = Lowest Cost Regions)",
    y = "Declared Income (₺)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

```

## 11.3 Average Rent Levels Across Income Quartiles

```{r}
df %>%
  mutate(income_group = ntile(Edevlet_Net_Gelir, 4)) %>%
  group_by(income_group) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_rent = mean(kira_il_ortalama, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

```

## 11.4 — Mean Rent by Income Quartile

```{r}
df %>%
  mutate(income_quartile = ntile(Edevlet_Net_Gelir, 4)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(income_quartile), y = kira_il_ortalama)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = "mean", fill = "#7E57C2") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Rent Levels Across Income Quartiles",
    x = "Income Quartile",
    y = "Average Rent (₺)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)


```

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

rent_summary <- model_data_scaled %>%
mutate(income_group = ntile(Edevlet_Net_Gelir, 4)) %>%
group_by(income_group) %>%
summarise(
avg_rent = mean(kira_il_ortalama, na.rm = TRUE),
sd_rent  = sd(kira_il_ortalama,  na.rm = TRUE),
n        = n(),
se_rent  = sd_rent / sqrt(n)
)

ggplot(rent_summary, aes(x = factor(income_group), y = avg_rent)) +
geom_col(fill = "#00BFC4", alpha = 0.9) +
geom_errorbar(
aes(ymin = avg_rent - se_rent, ymax = avg_rent + se_rent),
width = 0.15,
linewidth = 0.7
) +
labs(
title    = "Average Rent by Income Quartiles",
subtitle = "Bars show mean rent; error bars show ±1 SE",
x        = "Income quartile (based on Edevlet_Net_Gelir)",
y        = "Average monthly rent (TL)"
) +
scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
theme_bw(base_size = 16)
```
